chapter: Ch 5 — The Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 3 · LLP as a body corporate
questions.stem: Under section 3 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008, an LLP is:

readLink.label: Read: What an LLP is, s. 3 →

options.text: An association of persons which becomes a legal person only when its partners so agree in the LLP agreement
options.explanation: Legal personality comes from the statute on registration, not from the partners' agreement; s. 3(1) confers it directly.

options.text: A body corporate formed and incorporated under the Act and a legal entity separate from that of its partners, with perpetual succession
options.explanation: Correct. Section 3(1) makes the LLP a body corporate and a separate legal entity, s. 3(2) gives it perpetual succession, and s. 3(3) says a change in partners does not affect its existence, rights or liabilities.

options.text: A firm within the meaning of section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932, with the added feature of limited liability
options.explanation: Section 4 of the LLP Act expressly switches the Partnership Act 1932 off; an LLP is not a firm under the 1932 Act at all.

options.text: An unincorporated association whose property is held by the partners jointly
options.explanation: The LLP owns its own property under s. 14(b); the partners hold nothing jointly in the way partners of a firm do.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 4 · Non-application of the Partnership Act
questions.stem: Ganesh argues that a partner of an LLP is entitled to six per cent interest on an advance he made to the LLP, relying on section 13(d) of the Indian Partnership Act 1932. The LLP agreement is silent on interest. His argument:

readLink.label: Read: Why a third form was needed, s. 4 →

options.text: Succeeds, because the 1932 Act applies to every partnership in India
options.explanation: The 1932 Act applies to firms constituted under it. Section 4 of the LLP Act removes it from LLPs.

options.text: Succeeds, because the First Schedule reproduces the 1932 Act defaults
options.explanation: The First Schedule is a separate and shorter list of its own; it does not reproduce ss. 12 and 13 of the 1932 Act.

options.text: Fails, because section 4 provides that the Indian Partnership Act 1932 shall not apply to an LLP, and the First Schedule contains no interest provision
options.explanation: Correct. Section 4 switches the 1932 Act off save as otherwise provided, and the First Schedule that fills gaps under s. 23(4) says nothing about interest on contribution or on advances. Interest must be written into the LLP agreement.

options.text: Fails, but only because he did not obtain the consent of the other partners before making the advance
options.explanation: Consent is not the defect. Even a fully consented advance carries no statutory interest in an LLP.

questions.stem: The partners of an LLP settle their profit-sharing ratio at a meeting and record it only in the minutes; nothing is signed as an agreement. For the purposes of section 2(1)(o):

readLink.label: Read: What an LLP is, s. 2(1)(o) →

options.text: There is no LLP agreement on that matter, because s. 2(1)(o) requires a written agreement between the partners or between the LLP and its partners, so the First Schedule default applies
options.explanation: Correct. The definition is expressly of a written agreement, and s. 23(4) then supplies the First Schedule provision for any matter the agreement does not deal with — here, an equal share.

options.text: The minutes are conclusive, because clause 8 of the First Schedule requires decisions to be minuted
options.explanation: Clause 8 requires minutes to be kept; it does not turn a minute into the written LLP agreement the definition demands.

options.text: An oral agreement suffices, since the Act nowhere requires writing
options.explanation: It does. The words 'any written agreement' are part of the definition in s. 2(1)(o).

options.text: The ratio binds the partners but not the LLP, because the LLP was not a party
options.explanation: The problem is the absence of writing, not the absence of the LLP as a party; s. 2(1)(o) contemplates agreements between partners alone as well.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a 'body corporate' for the purposes of section 2(1)(e) of the LLP Act 2008?

readLink.label: Read: What an LLP is, s. 2(1)(e) →

options.text: An LLP incorporated outside India
options.explanation: Expressly included by s. 2(1)(e)(ii) in the inclusive limb of the definition.

options.text: A company incorporated outside India
options.explanation: Expressly included by s. 2(1)(e)(iii).

options.text: An LLP registered under the LLP Act 2008
options.explanation: Expressly included by s. 2(1)(e)(i); this is what allows one LLP to be a partner in another.

options.text: A co-operative society registered under a State co-operative societies Act
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(1)(e) expressly excludes a corporation sole, a co-operative society registered under any law, and any other body corporate notified by the Central Government as excluded.

questions.stem: Sanchari Media LLP is incorporated on 12 November 2026. Under the proviso to the definition of 'financial year' in section 2(1)(l), its first financial year may end on:

readLink.label: Read: What an LLP is, s. 2(1)(l) →

options.text: 31 March 2027, because a financial year always runs to the next 31 March
options.explanation: That is the ordinary rule, but the proviso gives an LLP incorporated after 30 September the option of a longer first period.

options.text: 31 March 2028, because the LLP was incorporated after 30 September 2026 and the proviso allows the first financial year to end on 31 March of the year next following
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 2(1)(l) permits an LLP incorporated after 30 September of a year to run its first financial year to 31 March of the year next following, giving a first period of about seventeen months.

options.text: 11 November 2027, twelve months from incorporation
options.explanation: The Act defines the financial year by reference to 1 April and 31 March, not by reference to the anniversary of incorporation.

options.text: Any date the partners choose in the LLP agreement
options.explanation: The financial year is fixed by the statutory definition; the agreement cannot vary it.

questions.stem: An LLP has a contribution of ₹22,00,000 and a turnover of ₹47,00,000 as per its Statement of Account and Solvency for the immediately preceding financial year. On the basis of section 2(1)(ta), it is:

readLink.label: Read: What an LLP is, s. 2(1)(ta) →

options.text: A small LLP, because its contribution is below ₹25,00,000
options.explanation: The definition has two limbs and both must be satisfied; the turnover limb fails.

options.text: A small LLP, because either limb alone is enough
options.explanation: This confuses the small-LLP test, which is cumulative, with the audit test, which is triggered by either limb.

options.text: Not a small LLP, because the definition requires the contribution not to exceed ₹25,00,000 AND the turnover not to exceed ₹40,00,000, and the turnover limb fails
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(1)(ta) is cumulative. Because the LLP is not a small LLP it does not get the half-penalty benefit of s. 76A.

options.text: Not a small LLP, because a small LLP must also have only two partners
options.explanation: The definition says nothing about the number of partners; it is a contribution and turnover test.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 26 with s. 18 of 1932 Act · Agency
questions.stem: The single structural difference from which the limited liability of an LLP partner follows is that a partner of an LLP is:

readLink.label: Read: LLP compared with a partnership firm →

options.text: Not an agent of anybody, so he can bind nobody
options.explanation: He plainly is an agent — of the LLP — and can bind it for the purposes of its business.

options.text: An agent of the other partners but not of the LLP
options.explanation: This reverses the section. Section 26 makes him the agent of the LLP.

options.text: An agent of the LLP and of the other partners, but only within the limits set by the LLP agreement
options.explanation: The agency of co-partners is exactly what s. 26 removes; and internal limits do not by themselves bind an outsider (s. 27(1)).

options.text: The agent of the LLP for the purpose of its business, but NOT of the other partners
options.explanation: Correct. Section 18 of the 1932 Act makes a partner the agent of the firm and of the other partners; s. 26 keeps the first limb and deletes the second, and that deletion is the whole of limited liability.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 7, 23 · LLP compared with a company
questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts an LLP with a company registered under the Companies Act 2013?

readLink.label: Read: LLP compared with a company →

options.text: An LLP need hold no statutory meetings, whereas a company must hold board and general meetings; and in an LLP every partner may take part in management, whereas a member of a company does not manage it
options.explanation: Correct. The LLP Act prescribes no meetings at all, and clause 4 of the First Schedule lets every partner manage, while a company is managed by its Board and a member as such is not its agent.

options.text: Both an LLP and a company must have a common seal
options.explanation: Section 14(c) makes the common seal optional for an LLP ('if it decides to have one').

options.text: A partner of an LLP is not an agent of the LLP, just as a member is not an agent of the company
options.explanation: Section 26 makes every partner an agent of the LLP; that is a real difference from a company member, not a similarity.

options.text: An LLP is governed by a memorandum and articles of association
options.explanation: Its constitutional document is the LLP agreement under s. 23, with the First Schedule filling any gap.

questions.stem: Meghna Exports LLP moved its registered office and completed all the requirements on 4 May 2026, but filed the notice of change with the Registrar only much later. The default under section 13 continued for 132 days. The penalty to which the LLP is liable under section 13(4) is:

readLink.label: Read: Name and registered office, s. 13 →

options.explanation: This is 132 × ₹500 with the statutory cap ignored. Section 13(4) caps the penalty at ₹50,000 for the LLP and at ₹50,000 for every partner.
This applies the ₹100 a day rate that belongs to s. 69 (additional fee on late filing) and to s. 10, not the ₹500 a day rate in s. 13(4).

options.text: ₹500, a single default being one contravention
options.explanation: The section fixes ₹500 for EACH DAY during which the default continues; it is not a one-off sum.

Correct. The daily penalty of ₹500 for 132 days works out to ₹66,000, but s. 13(4) subjects it to a maximum of ₹50,000 for the LLP, so ₹50,000 is payable. An equal cap applies separately to every partner.

questions.stem: The statement filed along with the incorporation document under section 11(1)(c), that all the requirements of the Act and the rules in respect of incorporation have been complied with, must be made by:

readLink.label: Read: Incorporation, s. 11 →

options.text: Any two of the proposed partners
options.explanation: Subscribers alone will not do; the section requires a professional as well.

options.text: An advocate, a Company Secretary, a Chartered Accountant or a Cost Accountant engaged in the formation of the LLP, AND anyone who subscribed his name to the incorporation document
options.explanation: Correct. Section 11(1)(c) requires the statement to be made by both — a named professional engaged in the formation and a subscriber to the incorporation document.

options.text: The Registrar of the State in which the registered office is to be situated
options.explanation: The Registrar receives the statement; he does not make it. Section 12(2) lets him accept it as sufficient evidence.

options.text: A practising Chartered Accountant alone, and no one else
options.explanation: The professional's statement is one half of the requirement; a subscriber must join in it, and three other professions are equally eligible.

questions.stem: A creditor of Rasika Foods LLP wishes to argue in a suit that the LLP was never validly formed, because one subscriber to the incorporation document had no intention of carrying on business. Against the certificate of incorporation issued under section 12(1)(b), his argument is:

readLink.label: Read: Incorporation, s. 12 →

options.text: Good, because the Registrar's satisfaction is only prima facie
options.explanation: Section 12(2) lets the Registrar accept the professional's statement as sufficient evidence, but s. 12(4) then makes the certificate conclusive, not prima facie.

options.text: Good, because s. 11(1)(a) is a mandatory requirement
options.explanation: It is mandatory, and non-compliance may have consequences for the person who made a false statement under s. 11(3); it does not let a third party unravel the incorporation.

options.text: Good only if he brings it within fourteen days of registration
options.explanation: The fourteen days in s. 12(1) is the Registrar's own time limit for acting; it is not a window for challenging the certificate.

options.text: Bad, because section 12(4) makes the certificate conclusive evidence that the LLP is incorporated by the name specified in it
options.explanation: Correct. Once the certificate is issued, no one may argue in any proceeding that the LLP does not exist or that a step in its formation was defective; the remedy for a false s. 11(1)(c) statement lies in s. 11(3) against the maker.

questions.stem: On registration, an LLP by its name becomes capable of doing all of the following EXCEPT:

readLink.label: Read: Incorporation, s. 14 →

options.text: Suing and being sued
options.explanation: Expressly conferred by s. 14(a).

options.text: Acquiring, owning, holding and disposing of movable and immovable, tangible and intangible property
options.explanation: Expressly conferred by s. 14(b).

options.text: Being compelled to adopt a common seal
options.explanation: Correct. Section 14(c) allows an LLP to have a common seal 'if it decides to have one'. The seal is optional, so this is the one thing in the list the section does not require.

options.text: Doing and suffering such other acts and things as bodies corporate may lawfully do and suffer
options.explanation: Expressly conferred by s. 14(d).

questions.stem: On an application under section 16, the Registrar reserves a name for a proposed LLP. The reservation lasts for:

readLink.label: Read: Name and registered office, s. 16 →

options.text: Three months from the date of intimation by the Registrar
options.explanation: Correct. Section 16(2) reserves the name for three months from the date of intimation, whether the applicant is forming a new LLP or changing the name of an existing one.

options.text: Twenty days from the date of the application
options.explanation: There is no twenty-day period in s. 16.

options.text: Six months, matching the period in section 34(2)
options.explanation: Six months is the Statement of Account and Solvency period in s. 34(2) and has nothing to do with name reservation.

options.text: Until the LLP is incorporated, with no outer limit
options.explanation: The section fixes an outer limit precisely so that names are not blocked indefinitely.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · First Schedule cl. 1 · Default profit share
questions.stem: Ashwini, Bharath and Chandana form an LLP with contributions of ₹15,00,000, ₹9,00,000 and ₹6,00,000 respectively. The LLP agreement filed with the Registrar deals only with the business and the registered office and says nothing about profits. The distributable profit for the year is ₹18,90,000. Chandana's share of that profit is:

readLink.label: Read: The LLP agreement and the First Schedule →

options.explanation: Correct. Section 23(4) applies the First Schedule to any matter on which the agreement is silent, and clause 1 gives all the partners an equal share of capital, profits and losses whatever each contributed: ₹18,90,000 ÷ 3 = ₹6,30,000.
This shares the profit in the contribution ratio 15:9:6, which is the rule students import from elsewhere. Clause 1 says 'equally', and contribution is irrelevant to it.
This is the contribution-ratio share of Ashwini, not of Chandana, and it applies the wrong rule as well as to the wrong partner.
This is the contribution-ratio share of Bharath. The contribution ratio does not govern at all where the agreement is silent.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 15 · Name of an LLP
questions.stem: Which of the following names could NOT be registered for an LLP?

readLink.label: Read: Name and registered office, s. 15 →

options.text: Devaki Consultants LLP
options.explanation: It ends with the acronym 'LLP' as s. 15(1) requires and raises no s. 15(2) objection on the facts given.

options.text: LLP Devaki Consultants
options.explanation: Correct. Section 15(1) requires the words 'limited liability partnership' or the acronym 'LLP' to be the LAST words of the name. Placing the acronym first does not satisfy the section.

options.text: Devaki Consultants Limited Liability Partnership
options.explanation: The full words appear as the last words of the name, which is the alternative s. 15(1) expressly permits.

options.text: Devaki and Sons Trading LLP
options.explanation: The form of the name is unobjectionable; only an undesirable or too-nearly-resembling name is caught by s. 15(2).

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 5 · Who may be a partner
questions.stem: Which of these persons is disqualified from becoming a partner in an LLP under section 5?

readLink.label: Read: Partners, s. 5 →

options.text: A private limited company
options.explanation: Section 5 expressly allows a body corporate to be a partner; only individuals are touched by the proviso.

options.text: An individual who was adjudged insolvent in 2019 and obtained his discharge in 2023
options.explanation: The bar is on an UNDISCHARGED insolvent. A discharged insolvent is not disqualified.

options.text: An individual who has applied to be adjudicated an insolvent and whose application is still pending
options.explanation: Correct. Clause (c) of the proviso to s. 5 disqualifies a person who has applied to be adjudicated an insolvent while the application is pending, alongside the undischarged insolvent in clause (b) and the person found of unsound mind in clause (a).

options.text: Another LLP registered under the Act
options.explanation: An LLP is a body corporate under s. 2(1)(e)(i) and may therefore be a partner in another LLP.

questions.stem: The number of partners in an LLP falls below two. Section 6(2) makes the sole partner personally liable only where:

readLink.label: Read: Partners, s. 6 →

options.text: The LLP carries on business at all while the number is reduced, from the first day
options.explanation: The section gives a grace period; liability attaches only to obligations incurred after more than six months.

options.text: The Tribunal has first ordered the LLP to be wound up under s. 64(b)
options.explanation: The two provisions are independent. Section 6(2) operates by itself and needs no order; s. 64(b) merely gives the Tribunal a ground.

options.text: The sole partner is also a designated partner
options.explanation: Designated-partner status is irrelevant to s. 6(2); it goes to ss. 8 and 10.

options.text: The LLP carries on business for more than six months while so reduced, the person is the only partner during that time, and he knows the business is being carried on with him alone — and then only for obligations incurred during that period
options.explanation: Correct. All four limbs must be present, and the liability is confined to obligations incurred after the six months have run out. It is additional to the LLP's own liability and does not dissolve the LLP.

questions.stem: Trikuta Ventures LLP has three partners, all of which are private limited companies. On the requirement of designated partners, section 7(1) means that:

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners and the DPIN, s. 7 →

options.text: At least two individuals who are nominees of those bodies corporate must act as designated partners, and at least one of them must be resident in India, meaning he has stayed in India for not less than 120 days during the financial year
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 7(1) covers exactly this case: where all the partners are bodies corporate, two individuals who are partners or nominees of those bodies corporate act as designated partners. The Explanation, as amended in 2021, sets the residence test at 120 days in the financial year.

options.text: The three companies themselves become the designated partners
options.explanation: A designated partner must be an individual; a body corporate can never itself be one.

options.text: No designated partner is needed, because there is no individual partner
options.explanation: The proviso exists precisely to prevent that result.

options.text: At least two individuals must be designated partners and BOTH must be resident in India for at least 182 days
options.explanation: Only one need be resident, and the 2021 amendment reduced the residence test from 182 days to 120 days.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 9 · Vacancy among designated partners
questions.stem: One of the two designated partners of an LLP resigns and the LLP appoints nobody in his place. The immediate legal consequence under section 9 is:

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners and the DPIN, s. 9 →

options.text: The LLP stands dissolved for want of the statutory minimum
options.explanation: Nothing in the Act dissolves an LLP for a shortfall in designated partners; s. 3(2) gives it perpetual succession.

options.text: Each partner is deemed to be a designated partner, and so carries the section 8 responsibilities including liability for penalties imposed on the LLP
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 9 deems every partner to be a designated partner where there is no designated partner or only one, which spreads the s. 8 compliance duty and the s. 8(b) exposure across all of them.

options.text: Nothing happens until six months have passed
options.explanation: Six months is the s. 6(2) and s. 64(b) period for a shortfall in PARTNERS, not designated partners; s. 9 gives thirty days to fill the vacancy.

options.text: The remaining designated partner alone becomes liable, and the other partners are protected
options.explanation: The proviso does the opposite: it draws every partner into designated-partner status.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 8 · Liabilities of a designated partner
questions.stem: An LLP fails to file its annual return and a penalty is imposed on the LLP. Nikhil, a designated partner who was abroad and had asked a colleague to attend to the filing, argues that he is not liable. Under section 8:

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners and the DPIN, s. 8 →

options.text: He is right, because liability follows the person who actually failed to file
options.explanation: Section 8(b) does not turn on who physically failed; it attaches to the office.

options.text: He is right, because a designated partner is liable only for penalties imposed on him personally
options.explanation: Clause (b) says in terms that he is liable to all penalties imposed on the LLP for contravention of the Act's provisions.

options.text: He is wrong: a designated partner is responsible for the doing of all acts required to be done by the LLP to comply with the Act, and is liable to all penalties imposed on the LLP for contravening those provisions
options.explanation: Correct. Section 8(a) puts the compliance duty on him and s. 8(b) puts the LLP's penalties on him as well. Delegating the work internally does not shift the statutory responsibility.

options.text: He is wrong, but only if the LLP agreement named him as the partner responsible for filings
options.explanation: The agreement may specify additional duties, but s. 8 operates whether or not the agreement says anything.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 24(5) · Entitlement of a former partner
questions.stem: Rohit is one of four partners in an LLP whose agreement is silent on what a retiring partner receives. He had agreed to contribute ₹10,00,000 but had actually paid in only ₹7,50,000. He ceases to be a partner on 30 November 2026, when the accumulated profits of the LLP stand at ₹22,00,000 and the accumulated losses at ₹6,00,000. Under section 24(5) he is entitled to receive:

readLink.label: Read: Cessation and changes in partners, s. 24 →

options.explanation: This uses the ₹10,00,000 he agreed to contribute. Section 24(5)(a) gives him only the capital contribution ACTUALLY MADE, which is ₹7,50,000.
This adds ₹7,50,000 to a quarter of the accumulated profits of ₹22,00,000 without deducting the accumulated losses. Section 24(5)(b) requires the losses to come off first.

Correct. Contribution actually made ₹7,50,000, plus his share of accumulated profits net of accumulated losses at the date of cessation: (₹22,00,000 − ₹6,00,000) ÷ 4 = ₹4,00,000. Total ₹11,50,000. The equal division comes from clause 1 of the First Schedule, the agreement being silent.
This gives him only the contribution and ignores s. 24(5)(b), which adds his right to share in the accumulated profits net of losses.

questions.stem: Before their LLP was incorporated, the subscribers signed a written agreement with a landlord committing the proposed LLP to a five-year lease. After incorporation the partners never discussed it. Under section 23(3), the LLP is:

readLink.label: Read: The LLP agreement and the First Schedule, s. 23 →

options.text: Bound, because a pre-incorporation agreement in writing binds the LLP automatically
options.explanation: Section 23(3) makes the obligation conditional; it is not automatic.

options.text: Bound, because the subscribers became the partners on incorporation under s. 22
options.explanation: Section 22 identifies who the partners are; it does not ratify their pre-incorporation promises on behalf of the LLP.

options.text: Not bound, because the LLP Act nowhere permits a pre-incorporation agreement to impose obligations on an LLP
options.explanation: It does permit it — s. 23(3) says such an agreement 'may impose obligations on the LLP'. The defect here is the missing condition, not the absence of a power.

options.text: Not bound, because a written pre-incorporation agreement imposes obligations on the LLP only if it is ratified by all the partners after incorporation, and it was not
options.explanation: Correct. Section 23(3) permits pre-incorporation obligations but only on ratification by all the partners after incorporation; without ratification the agreement binds its signatories alone, the LLP not having existed to contract.

questions.stem: The LLP agreement of Anantha Studios LLP describes Vidya as the 'managing partner' but fixes no remuneration for her. She claims a salary for running the business. Her claim:

readLink.label: Read: The LLP agreement and the First Schedule →

options.text: Fails, because clause 5 of the First Schedule provides that no partner is entitled to remuneration for acting in the business or management of the LLP, and the agreement is silent on pay
options.explanation: Correct. The title confers the role; only an express provision in the LLP agreement can confer the pay. Clause 5 is the default on a silent agreement.

options.text: Succeeds, because clause 4 entitles every partner to take part in management and management implies remuneration
options.explanation: Clause 4 gives the right to manage. Clause 5, in the very next line, denies remuneration for doing so.

options.text: Succeeds, because a managing partner is an employee of the LLP
options.explanation: A partner acting in the business of the LLP is not thereby its employee, and the Act creates no such implied contract of employment.

options.text: Fails, because remuneration to a partner is prohibited by the Act altogether
options.explanation: Not prohibited — merely not the default. The partners may agree on remuneration and record it in the LLP agreement.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · First Schedule cl. 6, cl. 7 · Decision making
questions.stem: An LLP has five partners and an agreement that is silent on decision making. Three of them wish to admit a sixth partner and also to change the nature of the business from trading to manufacture. Under the First Schedule:

readLink.label: Read: The LLP agreement and the First Schedule →

options.text: Both decisions carry, because three out of five is a majority
options.explanation: A bare majority is enough for ordinary matters but not for either of these two.

options.text: Neither decision carries: admitting a partner needs the consent of ALL the existing partners under clause 6, and changing the nature of the business needs the consent of ALL the partners under the proviso to clause 7
options.explanation: Correct. Clause 7 makes ordinary matters a question for a majority in number, each partner having one vote, but it expressly carves out a change in the nature of the business; and clause 6 separately requires unanimity to introduce a partner.

options.text: Both decisions carry if the three hold the larger part of the contribution
options.explanation: Voting under clause 7 is by a majority IN NUMBER, one vote per partner; the size of a partner's contribution is irrelevant.

options.text: The admission carries but the change of business does not
options.explanation: The admission is the one that clearly fails, clause 6 requiring the consent of all existing partners.

questions.stem: The LLP agreement of Poorvi Traders LLP says nothing about how a partner may resign. Shyam wishes to leave. Section 24(1) requires him to:

readLink.label: Read: Cessation and changes in partners, s. 24 →

options.text: File a notice with the Registrar at least thirty days in advance
options.explanation: The Registrar filing is the LLP's obligation under s. 25(2)(a), within thirty days AFTER the cessation; s. 24(1) is about notice to the other partners.

options.text: Obtain the consent of all the other partners
options.explanation: Consent is needed to ADMIT a partner (First Schedule cl. 6); a partner may leave on notice without it.

options.text: Give a notice in writing of not less than thirty days to the other partners of his intention to resign
options.explanation: Correct. Section 24(1) allows cessation in accordance with an agreement with the other partners, and in the absence of such an agreement by not less than thirty days' written notice to the other partners.

options.text: Give three months' notice, matching the period in section 17
options.explanation: Three months in s. 17 is the time to comply with a direction to change the LLP's name and has nothing to do with resignation.

questions.stem: Ismail ceased to be a partner of an LLP on 2 March 2026. Neither he nor the LLP filed any notice, and on 20 March 2026 a supplier who had dealt with the LLP for years, and who did not know of the change, extended credit believing Ismail to be a partner. Under section 24(3):

readLink.label: Read: Cessation and changes in partners, s. 24 →

options.text: Ismail is protected, because cessation takes effect on the date agreed between the partners
options.explanation: It does take effect between the partners on that date; s. 24(3) deals separately with the position as against outsiders.

options.text: Ismail is protected, because a former partner is never liable for acts after his cessation
options.explanation: That is the effect of s. 24(3) only once one of its two exceptions is satisfied, and neither is on these facts.

options.text: Ismail is protected only if the LLP had at least two other partners on 20 March 2026
options.explanation: The number of remaining partners is irrelevant to s. 24(3); it goes to s. 6.

options.text: Ismail is to be regarded, in relation to the supplier, as still being a partner, because the supplier had no notice of the cessation and no notice of it had been delivered to the Registrar
options.explanation: Correct. Section 24(3) protects a former partner only where the person dealing with the LLP has notice, or notice has reached the Registrar. Either limb suffices, and s. 25(6) lets the former partner file that notice himself if he fears the LLP will not.

questions.stem: Kavya, a partner in an LLP, changes her residential address. The time limits in section 25 are:

readLink.label: Read: Cessation and changes in partners, s. 25 →

options.text: Kavya must inform the LLP within fifteen days of the change, and the LLP must file a notice with the Registrar within thirty days of the change
options.explanation: Correct. Section 25(1) puts a fifteen-day duty on the partner towards the LLP; s. 25(2)(b) puts a thirty-day duty on the LLP towards the Registrar. The two clocks both start from the change, so the LLP's window is not extended by a late intimation.

options.text: Kavya must inform the Registrar within fifteen days, and the LLP need do nothing
options.explanation: A partner's duty under s. 25(1) runs to the LLP, not to the Registrar, and the LLP has its own filing duty.

options.text: Both Kavya and the LLP have thirty days from the change
options.explanation: The partner's period is fifteen days; only the LLP's is thirty.

options.text: Kavya must inform the LLP within thirty days and the LLP must file within sixty days
options.explanation: Sixty days is the annual return period in s. 35; it appears nowhere in s. 25.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 26, 28 · Liability for a co-partner's act
questions.stem: Two partners of a design LLP work on unrelated projects. One of them prepares a negligent structural report and the client sues both partners personally as well as the LLP. On the personal claim against the partner who had nothing to do with the report:

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability of the LLP and of a partner →

options.text: He is liable, because partners are jointly and severally liable for all acts of the entity
options.explanation: That is s. 25 of the Partnership Act 1932, which s. 4 of the LLP Act puts out of play.

options.text: He is not liable: section 28(2) provides expressly that a partner shall not be personally liable for the wrongful act or omission of any other partner of the LLP
options.explanation: Correct. The LLP is liable under s. 27(2) because the omission was in the course of its business; the partner who made it is personally liable under the first half of s. 28(2); and the other partner is protected by its second half and by s. 28(1).

options.text: He is liable to the extent of his contribution
options.explanation: There is no contribution-limited liability in the Act; s. 28(1) removes personal liability arising solely from being a partner, and it does so entirely.

options.text: He is liable unless he proves he took reasonable care
options.explanation: No such burden is placed on him. Section 28(2) is a flat rule, not a defence he must establish.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 27(1) · When the LLP is not bound
questions.stem: A partner exceeds a limit in the LLP agreement and signs a contract with a supplier who has always dealt with the LLP and knows nothing of the limit. Under section 27(1), the LLP is:

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability of the LLP and of a partner →

options.text: Not bound, because the partner in fact had no authority
options.explanation: That is only the first of two cumulative limbs. Both must be satisfied before the LLP escapes.

options.text: Not bound, because a restriction in the LLP agreement is filed with the Registrar and so notice of it is imputed to everyone
options.explanation: The Act attaches no constructive-notice consequence to the filing of an LLP agreement; s. 27(1)(b) asks about the outsider's actual state of knowledge.

options.text: Bound, because the LLP escapes only where the partner had no authority AND the person either knew of the want of authority or did not know or believe him to be a partner — and neither of those is true here
options.explanation: Correct. Section 27(1) is conjunctive. The supplier neither knew of the restriction nor doubted that the man was a partner, so the LLP is bound and the breach of the internal limit is a matter between the partners.

options.text: Bound, but only up to the limit stated in the LLP agreement
options.explanation: Section 27(1) makes the LLP bound or not bound; it does not scale the obligation down to the internal ceiling.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 34(4) with the rules · Audit threshold
questions.stem: For the financial year ended 31 March 2027, Nandana Foods LLP has a turnover of ₹42,60,000 and a total contribution of ₹18,00,000. On the audit requirement:

readLink.label: Read: Accounts, audit, SAS and the annual return →

options.text: No audit is required, because the contribution of ₹18,00,000 is below ₹25,00,000
options.explanation: The contribution limb is satisfied but the turnover limb is not, and either limb alone brings the LLP into audit.

options.text: An audit is required, because the turnover exceeds ₹40,00,000 — either limb alone triggers the requirement
options.explanation: Correct. Turnover of ₹42,60,000 is above the ₹40,00,000 threshold, so the accounts must be audited even though the contribution of ₹18,00,000 is comfortably below ₹25,00,000.

options.text: No audit is required, because both the turnover and the contribution limits must be exceeded before an audit becomes compulsory
options.explanation: That cumulative reading belongs to the small-LLP definition in s. 2(1)(ta). The audit test is triggered by either limb.

options.text: An audit is required only if the partners pass a resolution to that effect
options.explanation: A voluntary audit is possible, but here the statutory threshold has been crossed and the audit is compulsory whatever the partners decide.

questions.stem: Sthira Infratech LLP closes its financial year on 31 March 2027. The last date for filing its annual return with the Registrar under section 35 is:

readLink.label: Read: Accounts, audit, SAS and the annual return →

options.explanation: This counts sixty days as two calendar months. Sixty days from 31 March 2027 falls one day earlier, because April has thirty days and May has thirty-one.

options.text: 30 September 2027
options.explanation: This is the six-month date for PREPARING the Statement of Account and Solvency under s. 34(2), not the annual return date.

options.text: 30 October 2027
options.explanation: This is the date for FILING the Statement of Account and Solvency — thirty days after the six months expire — not the annual return date.
Correct. Section 35 gives sixty days from the closure of the financial year. Counting from 31 March 2027, thirty days reaches 30 April and the next thirty reach 30 May 2027.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 34(3), 69 · Late filing of the SAS
questions.stem: Sthira Infratech LLP, whose financial year ended on 31 March 2027, was required to file its Statement of Account and Solvency within thirty days from the end of six months from the close of that year. It filed on 6 December 2027. The additional fee payable under section 69 is:

readLink.label: Read: Accounts, audit, SAS and the annual return →

options.explanation: Correct. Six months from 31 March 2027 expires on 30 September 2027, and thirty days from then gives a due date of 30 October 2027. From 31 October to 6 December 2027 is 37 days of delay, and s. 69 charges ₹100 for every day of delay: 37 × ₹100 = ₹3,700.
This counts the delay from 30 September 2027, the date for PREPARING the statement, and ignores the further thirty days the rules allow for filing it.
This counts the delay from 30 May 2027, which is the annual return date under s. 35. The two filings run on different clocks.

options.text: ₹100, a single flat additional fee
options.explanation: Section 69 charges ₹100 for EVERY DAY of delay, not once.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 28 · Extent of liability of a partner
questions.stem: Which statement states section 28 correctly?

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability of the LLP and of a partner →

options.text: A partner has no liability of any kind once the LLP is registered
options.explanation: Section 28(2) preserves his liability for his own wrongful act or omission, and ss. 6(2), 29 and 30 add other routes to personal liability.

options.text: A partner is liable for every obligation of the LLP up to the amount of his contribution
options.explanation: There is no contribution-capped liability in the Act; s. 28(1) removes personal liability for the LLP's obligations altogether.

options.text: A partner is liable for the wrongful acts of his co-partners but not for the LLP's contracts
options.explanation: This reverses the section. He is not liable for a co-partner's wrongful act, and he is not liable for the LLP's contracts either.

options.text: A partner is not personally liable for an obligation of the LLP solely by reason of being a partner, but he remains personally liable for his own wrongful act or omission and is never liable for another partner's
options.explanation: Correct. Section 28(1) supplies the first half and s. 28(2) supplies both parts of the second, and together they define exactly how far the protection goes.

questions.stem: A retired banker allows an LLP to describe him as 'our senior partner' in its proposal documents, though he is not a partner. A lender advances money on the faith of that description. Under section 29:

readLink.label: Read: Holding out, fraud and whistle blowing, s. 29 →

options.text: He is liable to the lender, whether or not he knew that the representation had reached that lender; and the LLP is also liable to the extent of the credit it received or the financial benefit derived
options.explanation: Correct. Section 29(1) makes a person who knowingly permits himself to be represented as a partner liable to anyone who gave credit to the LLP on the faith of it, expressly whether or not he knew the representation reached that person, and the proviso adds the LLP's liability to the extent of the credit or benefit.

options.text: He is not liable, because he never signed anything
options.explanation: The section reaches representations by words spoken or written OR by conduct, including knowingly permitting a representation to be made.

options.text: He is liable only if he intended to deceive the lender
options.explanation: No intention to deceive is required; the section is satisfied by the representation, the credit and the reliance.

options.text: He is liable only if the LLP is first shown to be unable to pay
options.explanation: His liability under s. 29(1) is direct and does not depend on the LLP defaulting first.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 30 · Unlimited liability for fraud
questions.stem: A partner of an LLP raises supplier credit on invoices for services the LLP never intended to render. The other partners knew nothing. Under section 30(1):

readLink.label: Read: Holding out, fraud and whistle blowing, s. 30 →

options.text: The liability of every partner becomes unlimited, because the act was done in the name of the LLP
options.explanation: Only the LLP and the partners who acted with intent to defraud carry the unlimited liability; the innocent partners keep their s. 28(1) protection.

options.text: The liability of the guilty partner is unlimited for all or any of the debts of the LLP, and the LLP is liable to the same extent unless the LLP establishes that the act was without its knowledge or authority
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(1) makes the liability of the LLP and of the partners who acted with intent to defraud unlimited, and the proviso puts the burden of disproving knowledge or authority on the LLP.

options.text: The liability of the guilty partner is limited to the amount of the credit obtained
options.explanation: Section 30(1) makes it unlimited 'for all or any of the debts or other liabilities of the LLP', not merely for the sum defrauded.

options.text: Nothing follows until a court convicts him under section 30(2)
options.explanation: The civil consequence in s. 30(1) and the compensation in s. 30(3) operate independently of any conviction under s. 30(2).

questions.stem: An employee of an LLP gives information during an investigation which leads to a partner being convicted, and the LLP then demotes him. Section 31 provides that:

readLink.label: Read: Holding out, fraud and whistle blowing, s. 31 →

options.text: The employee is entitled to a share of any fine recovered
options.explanation: The section provides no reward out of the fine; the relief it gives is a reduction or waiver of penalty and protection from discrimination.

options.text: The Court or Tribunal must waive every penalty against him, and the demotion is void
options.explanation: The power in s. 31(1) is discretionary ('may reduce or waive'), and s. 31(2) prohibits the discrimination rather than declaring the demotion void.

options.text: The Court or Tribunal MAY reduce or waive any penalty leviable against him, and he may not be demoted, discharged, suspended or otherwise discriminated against merely for having given the information
options.explanation: Correct. Section 31(1) gives the Court or Tribunal a discretion to reduce or waive a penalty where useful information was given during an investigation or where information led to a conviction, and s. 31(2) forbids retaliation in the terms and conditions of employment or partnership.

options.text: The protection applies to partners only, not to employees
options.explanation: Section 31 speaks throughout of 'any partner or employee' of an LLP.

questions.stem: Which of the following may NOT be counted as a partner's contribution to an LLP under section 32?

readLink.label: Read: Contribution, s. 32 →

options.text: A promissory note given by the partner to the LLP
options.explanation: Expressly named in s. 32(1) among the permitted forms of contribution.

options.text: An agreement by the partner to contribute cash at a later date
options.explanation: Expressly named — 'other agreements to contribute cash or property'.

options.text: A contract for services the partner will perform in future
options.explanation: Expressly named — 'contracts for services performed or to be performed'. This is one of the genuine advantages of the LLP form.

options.text: A contribution whose monetary value is deliberately left out of the accounts of the LLP
options.explanation: Correct. Section 32(1) is very wide as to FORM, but s. 32(2) requires the monetary value of each partner's contribution to be accounted for and disclosed in the accounts in the prescribed manner. An undisclosed and unvalued contribution does not satisfy the section.

questions.stem: A lender advanced money to an LLP after reading in its filed LLP agreement that a partner was obliged to bring in a further ₹20,00,000. After the loan, the partners privately agreed among themselves to reduce that obligation to ₹5,00,000, and the lender was never told. Under section 33(2), the lender may:

readLink.label: Read: Contribution, s. 33 →

options.text: Enforce the original obligation of ₹20,00,000 against that partner, having extended credit in reliance on it without notice of the compromise
options.explanation: Correct. Section 33(2) lets a creditor who extended credit or otherwise acted in reliance on an obligation described in the LLP agreement, without notice of any compromise between the partners, enforce the ORIGINAL obligation.

options.text: Enforce only the reduced obligation of ₹5,00,000, because the agreement as amended governs
options.explanation: That is exactly the result s. 33(2) is written to prevent; the compromise does not bind a creditor who acted without notice of it.

options.text: Enforce nothing, because the obligation to contribute is owed to the LLP and not to him
options.explanation: Section 33(2) gives the creditor a direct route against the partner in these circumstances.

options.text: Enforce ₹20,00,000, but only after the LLP has been wound up
options.explanation: The section imposes no such precondition.

questions.stem: A partner assigns his entire right to share in the profits of an LLP to his sister. Under section 42, the sister:

readLink.label: Read: A partner's transferable interest, s. 42 →

options.text: Becomes a partner of the LLP in her brother's place
options.explanation: The assignment transfers economic rights only; becoming a partner is a separate step under s. 22 read with the LLP agreement.

options.text: Is entitled to the share of profits and to receive distributions, but is not entitled to participate in the management or conduct of the activities of the LLP or to access information about its transactions
options.explanation: Correct. Section 42(1) makes the economic rights transferable, and s. 42(3) withholds management participation and access to information from the transferee. The brother stays a partner: s. 42(2) says the transfer causes no disassociation.

options.text: Causes the LLP to be dissolved, the partner having parted with his interest
options.explanation: Section 42(2) says in terms that the transfer does not by itself cause the disassociation of the partner or a dissolution and winding up of the LLP.

options.text: Acquires nothing, because a partner's interest in an LLP is not transferable
options.explanation: It is transferable, wholly or in part, under s. 42(1).

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 55 to 57 · Who may convert
questions.stem: Which of the following may NOT convert itself into an LLP under Chapter X of the LLP Act 2008?

readLink.label: Read: Conversion into an LLP →

options.text: A firm registered under the Indian Partnership Act 1932
options.explanation: Section 55 read with the Second Schedule provides for exactly this conversion.

options.text: A private company
options.explanation: Section 56 read with the Third Schedule provides for it.

options.text: A listed public company
options.explanation: Correct. Section 57 permits an UNLISTED public company to convert; there is no provision for a listed company, and none for a sole proprietorship or a co-operative society either.

options.text: An unlisted public company
options.explanation: Section 57 read with the Fourth Schedule provides for it.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · Third and Fourth Schedules · Conditions
questions.stem: A private company with a subsisting charge on its plant and machinery in favour of its bank applies to convert into an LLP. All its shareholders are to be the partners. The application:

readLink.label: Read: Conversion into an LLP →

options.text: Succeeds, because the only condition is that all the shareholders become partners and no one else
options.explanation: That is one of two conditions in the Third Schedule; the other is not satisfied.

options.text: Succeeds, because a charge automatically vests in the LLP under section 58(3)(b)
options.explanation: Section 58(3)(b) governs what happens on conversion; it does not dispense with a condition precedent to conversion.

options.text: Fails, because a company can convert only after five years of incorporation
options.explanation: There is no such minimum period in the Act.

options.text: Fails, because the Third Schedule requires that there be no security interest in the assets of the company subsisting or in force at the time of the application
options.explanation: Correct. The Third Schedule (and the Fourth, for an unlisted public company) imposes two cumulative conditions: no subsisting security interest, and all the shareholders and no one else becoming the partners. The bank's charge must be satisfied or released first.

questions.stem: On and from the date specified in the certificate of registration issued on a conversion, section 58(3) provides that:

readLink.label: Read: Conversion into an LLP →

options.text: The whole undertaking of the firm or company, with all its property, assets, rights, liabilities and obligations, is transferred to and vests in the LLP without further assurance, act or deed, and the firm or company is deemed to be dissolved and removed from the records
options.explanation: Correct. Section 58(3)(b) effects the vesting by operation of law, so no separate conveyance is needed, and s. 58(3)(c) deems the converting entity dissolved and removed from the Registrar's records.

options.text: Each asset must be separately conveyed to the LLP by a registered instrument
options.explanation: The words 'without further assurance, act or deed' in s. 58(3)(b) are there precisely to avoid that.

options.text: The liabilities of the firm or company are extinguished, only its assets passing to the LLP
options.explanation: Liabilities and obligations vest along with the assets; conversion is not a way of shedding debt.

options.text: The firm or company continues in existence alongside the LLP for one year
options.explanation: It is deemed dissolved and removed from the records. What continues for twelve months is the statement of conversion on the LLP's official correspondence.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 64 · Winding up by the Tribunal
questions.stem: Which of the following is a ground on which the Tribunal may wind up an LLP under section 64?

readLink.label: Read: Winding up, foreign LLPs and compounding →

options.text: The LLP has failed to hold an annual general meeting
options.explanation: An LLP holds no statutory meetings at all, so there is no such ground.

options.text: The LLP has made default in filing the Statement of Account and Solvency or the annual return with the Registrar for any five consecutive financial years
options.explanation: Correct. This is the ground in s. 64. Note that it needs FIVE CONSECUTIVE financial years of default in either filing, so a single late filing is not enough.

options.text: The LLP is unable to pay its debts
options.explanation: That ground was OMITTED from s. 64 by the LLP (Amendment) Act 2021; the insolvency of an LLP is now dealt with under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016.

options.text: A partner has assigned his share of profits to an outsider
options.explanation: Section 42(2) says expressly that such a transfer causes no dissolution and winding up.

questions.stem: Under section 39 of the LLP Act 2008, compounding is available:

readLink.label: Read: Winding up, foreign LLPs and compounding →

options.text: For any offence under the Act, whatever the punishment
options.explanation: The section is confined to offences punishable with fine only.

options.text: For offences punishable with imprisonment, on payment of the maximum fine
options.explanation: An offence punishable with imprisonment, whether alone or with fine, cannot be compounded under s. 39.

options.text: Only for an offence punishable with fine only, by collecting a sum which may extend to the maximum fine provided for the offence and which shall not be lower than the minimum
options.explanation: Correct. Section 39 confines compounding to fine-only offences and fixes the compounding sum between the statutory minimum and maximum fine for that offence. The power is exercised by the Regional Director or an officer of that rank authorised by the Central Government.

options.text: Only where the Tribunal has first convicted the offender
options.explanation: Compounding operates instead of prosecution, not after conviction.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 26 to 30 · Case: four claims against one LLP
questions.case: Chitrakoot Advisory LLP has four partners — Bhavna, Dinesh, Farhan and Gayatri. Its LLP agreement provides that no partner may commit the LLP to any contract above ₹6,00,000 without a written resolution of all the partners. Four things happen during 2026. (i) Dinesh signs an equipment hire contract for ₹11,00,000 with a vendor who has supplied the LLP for six years and who has never been told of the internal limit. (ii) Farhan, carrying out a due-diligence assignment, negligently overlooks a registered charge, and the client suffers a loss of ₹34,00,000. (iii) Bhavna, acting with an outside associate and without the knowledge of the other partners, obtains ₹52,00,000 of supplier credit on invoices for work the LLP never intended to perform, and the money is shared between them. (iv) Gayatri's uncle, a retired civil servant, is described as 'our founding partner' on the LLP's tender documents; he has seen the documents and said nothing, and a financier lends the LLP ₹18,00,000 on the strength of his name.

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability of the LLP and of a partner →

questions.stem: On the ₹11,00,000 equipment hire contract signed by Dinesh, the position is:

options.text: The LLP is bound and must pay, because the LLP escapes under s. 27(1) only where the partner had no authority AND the vendor knew it or did not believe him to be a partner
options.explanation: Correct. Both limbs of s. 27(1) must be satisfied. The vendor neither knew of the internal cap nor doubted that Dinesh was a partner, so the LLP is bound; Dinesh's breach of the cap is a matter between the partners under the LLP agreement.

options.text: The LLP is not bound, because Dinesh acted beyond the limit in the LLP agreement
options.explanation: Want of actual authority is only the first limb of s. 27(1); by itself it does not release the LLP.

options.text: The LLP is bound only up to ₹6,00,000, the limit in the agreement
options.explanation: Section 27(1) makes the LLP bound or not bound; it does not scale the obligation down to the internal ceiling.

options.text: Dinesh alone is bound, as the LLP never authorised the contract
options.explanation: Section 26 makes him the agent of the LLP, and on these facts the agency binds the LLP; s. 27(3) then makes the obligation solely the LLP's.

questions.stem: On Farhan's negligent due diligence, the correct set of liabilities is:

options.text: The LLP alone is liable, a partner never being liable for a professional error
options.explanation: The first half of s. 28(2) preserves a partner's personal liability for his own wrongful act or omission.

options.text: All four partners are liable jointly and severally with the LLP
options.explanation: That is s. 25 of the Partnership Act 1932, which s. 4 of the LLP Act excludes.

options.text: The LLP is liable under s. 27(2) and Farhan is personally liable under s. 28(2), but Bhavna, Dinesh and Gayatri are not liable at all
options.explanation: Correct. Section 27(2) fixes the LLP because the omission was in the course of its business; the first half of s. 28(2) fixes Farhan for his own wrongful omission; and the second half of s. 28(2), with s. 28(1), keeps the other three out of it entirely.

options.text: Farhan is liable only up to his contribution to the LLP
options.explanation: Nothing in the Act caps a partner's liability for his own wrongful act at his contribution.

questions.stem: On the ₹52,00,000 of supplier credit obtained by Bhavna, section 30 means that:

options.text: Only the LLP is liable, and only to the extent of the credit obtained
options.explanation: Section 30(1) makes the liability unlimited for all or any of the debts of the LLP, and it reaches the guilty partner as well.

options.text: Bhavna's liability is unlimited for all or any of the debts of the LLP, and the LLP is liable to the same extent unless the LLP establishes that the act was without its knowledge or authority
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(1) makes the liability of the guilty partner unlimited, and the proviso places on the LLP the burden of proving the act was without its knowledge or authority — a burden it should discharge on these facts.

options.text: All four partners lose their limited liability, because the fraud was committed in the LLP's name
options.explanation: Section 30(1) reaches only the partners 'who acted with intent to defraud'; the innocent partners retain their s. 28(1) protection.

options.text: Nothing follows unless and until Bhavna is convicted under s. 30(2)
options.explanation: The unlimited civil liability in s. 30(1) and the compensation in s. 30(3) are independent of any prosecution.

questions.stem: On the ₹18,00,000 advanced by the financier on the strength of the uncle's name:

options.text: Gayatri is liable, because the person held out was her relative
options.explanation: Relationship is irrelevant; liability under s. 29 attaches to the person represented as a partner, and to anyone whose own act made the representation.

options.text: Nobody is liable, because the uncle never described himself as a partner
options.explanation: Section 29(1) catches a person who 'knowingly permits himself to be represented' as a partner, which is what he did by seeing the tender documents and saying nothing.

options.text: The uncle is liable only if he knew the representation had reached this particular financier
options.explanation: The section says expressly that it applies whether or not the person knows the representation has reached the person giving credit.

options.text: The uncle is personally liable to the financier under s. 29(1), and the LLP is liable in addition to the extent of the credit it received or the financial benefit derived on it
options.explanation: Correct. All three limbs are present — a representation knowingly permitted, credit given to the LLP, and reliance on the representation — and the proviso to s. 29(1) adds the LLP's liability to the extent of the credit or benefit.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 3, 6, 9, 24 · Case: an LLP down to one partner
questions.case: Neelambari Logistics LLP has exactly two partners, Padma and Raghav, both of whom are designated partners. The LLP agreement is silent on profit sharing and on what a former partner receives. Raghav dies on 14 April 2026. Padma continues the business alone, knows perfectly well that she is the only partner, and admits nobody. Between 15 April 2026 and 14 October 2026 the LLP incurs trade obligations of ₹11,50,000, and between 15 October 2026 and 31 March 2027 it incurs further trade obligations of ₹23,80,000. At the date of Raghav's death the accumulated profits of the LLP stood at ₹19,00,000 and the accumulated losses at ₹5,00,000; the contribution Raghav had actually paid in was ₹9,00,000.

readLink.label: Read: Partners, s. 6 →

questions.stem: The effect of Raghav's death on the existence of the LLP is that:

options.text: The LLP continues to exist, because it has perpetual succession and a change in its partners does not affect its existence, rights or liabilities; the shortfall merely gives the Tribunal a ground to wind it up after six months
options.explanation: Correct. Section 3(2) gives perpetual succession and s. 3(3) insulates the LLP from changes in its partners. Raghav's death is a cessation under s. 24(2)(a), not a dissolution, and s. 64(b) gives the Tribunal a discretionary ground once the number has been below two for more than six months.

options.text: The LLP stands dissolved automatically on 14 April 2026
options.explanation: Death dissolves a firm under the 1932 Act in certain circumstances; it does not dissolve a body corporate with perpetual succession.

options.text: The LLP stands dissolved automatically after six months
options.explanation: Section 64(b) creates a GROUND for the Tribunal to wind the LLP up. Somebody must invoke it, and the Tribunal must order it.

options.text: The LLP converts automatically into a sole proprietorship
options.explanation: The Act provides no such conversion; the LLP remains a body corporate registered under it.

questions.stem: As to designated partners after 14 April 2026, the position is:

options.text: Nothing needs to be done until the LLP admits a second partner
options.explanation: Section 9 gives thirty days to fill the vacancy, and s. 10(1) starts a penalty running for the s. 7(1) shortfall meanwhile.

options.text: Padma ceases to be a designated partner, there being no second one
options.explanation: The proviso to s. 9 does the opposite; it widens designated-partner status rather than removing it.

options.text: The LLP may appoint a designated partner within thirty days of the vacancy; because it has not, the s. 9 proviso deems every partner to be a designated partner, and the s. 10(1) penalty of ₹10,000 plus ₹100 for each further day runs against the LLP and against Padma
options.explanation: Correct. Section 9 gives thirty days, its proviso deems every partner a designated partner where there is only one or none, and s. 10(1) attaches the penalty for the continuing breach of s. 7(1), capped at ₹1,00,000 for the LLP and ₹50,000 for every partner.

options.text: Raghav's legal representative automatically becomes the second designated partner
options.explanation: A legal representative does not become a partner, still less a designated partner; s. 24(6) denies him even a right to interfere in management.

questions.stem: The amount of the LLP's trade obligations for which Padma is personally liable under section 6(2) is:
questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 6(2) · Personal liability of a sole partner

options.explanation: This makes Padma personally liable for everything incurred since the death. Section 6(2) attaches only to obligations incurred after the LLP has carried on business for MORE THAN six months while reduced below two.

Correct. Six months from 14 April 2026 expires on 14 October 2026. Only the obligations incurred after that — the ₹23,80,000 incurred between 15 October 2026 and 31 March 2027 — attract Padma's personal liability under s. 6(2). Her liability is additional to the LLP's, which remains liable for the whole ₹35,30,000.
This takes the obligations incurred INSIDE the first six months, which are exactly the ones s. 6(2) leaves as the sole obligation of the LLP under s. 27(3).

options.text: Nothing, because section 28(1) protects every partner
options.explanation: Section 28(1) removes liability arising solely from being a partner. Section 6(2) is a separate, express head of personal liability that operates despite it.

questions.stem: On the claim of Raghav's estate against the LLP, section 24 provides that the estate:
questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 24(5), 24(6) · Entitlement of a former partner

options.text: May demand that the LLP stop trading until it is paid
options.explanation: Section 24(6) denies a person entitled to a deceased partner's share any right to interfere in the management of the LLP.

options.text: Is entitled to nothing, the LLP agreement being silent
options.explanation: Silence is precisely when s. 24(5) applies; it operates 'unless otherwise provided in the LLP agreement'.

options.text: Is entitled to the contribution Raghav had AGREED to make, plus a share of the gross accumulated profits
options.explanation: Section 24(5)(a) gives the contribution ACTUALLY MADE, and s. 24(5)(b) gives a share of accumulated profits AFTER deducting accumulated losses.

options.text: Is entitled to the contribution actually made, ₹9,00,000, plus Raghav's share of the accumulated profits after deducting the accumulated losses as at 14 April 2026 — an equal half of ₹14,00,000, namely ₹7,00,000 — and has no right to interfere in the management
options.explanation: Correct. Section 24(5) gives the two components and fixes the valuation date at the date of cessation; clause 1 of the First Schedule makes the share equal, the agreement being silent; and s. 24(6) denies any management rights.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 55, 58, Second Schedule · Case: a firm converts
questions.case: Sahyadri Traders is a registered partnership firm with four partners — Anup, Bela, Chirag and Deepa. Deepa does not wish to be part of the proposed LLP. The firm has a cash-credit facility secured on its stock, a seven-year godown lease, a State excise licence, and a suit filed against it in 2024 by a transporter claiming ₹14,00,000 for services rendered in 2023. The partners apply to convert the firm into Sahyadri Traders LLP, and the Registrar issues a certificate of registration dated 20 August 2026.

readLink.label: Read: Conversion into an LLP →

questions.stem: On Deepa's wish to stay out of the LLP, the Second Schedule means that:
questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 55, Second Schedule · Composition condition

options.text: She may simply be omitted from the LLP, since the firm's other partners are in a majority
options.explanation: The Second Schedule requires the application to be made by all the partners of the firm; a majority will not do.

options.text: She must be omitted, because a converted LLP may not have more than three partners
options.explanation: There is no maximum number of partners for an LLP at all.

options.text: She cannot simply be left out: the application must be made by ALL the partners of the firm, and the partners of the LLP must comprise all the partners of the firm and no one else — so she must retire from the firm first, or come across and then resign under s. 24(1)
options.explanation: Correct. The Second Schedule imposes a strict composition condition in both directions: nobody may be dropped and nobody may be added as part of the conversion. Retiring from the firm before the application, or resigning from the LLP afterwards on thirty days' notice, are the two clean routes.

options.text: She may be left out provided the firm pays her out first
options.explanation: Payment does not cure the composition condition; what is needed is that she cease to be a partner of the FIRM before the application is made.

questions.stem: The last date on which the LLP must inform the Registrar of Firms of the conversion under section 58(2) is:
questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 58(2) · Intimation to the Registrar of Firms

options.text: 4 September 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 58(2) requires the LLP to inform the concerned Registrar of Firms within fifteen days of the date of registration. Counting fifteen days from, and excluding, 20 August 2026 gives 4 September 2026.

options.text: 19 September 2026
options.explanation: This applies a thirty-day period. Thirty days is the s. 25(2) period for changes in partners, not the s. 58(2) intimation period.

options.text: 20 August 2026, the same day
options.explanation: The section allows fifteen days; it does not require same-day intimation.

options.text: 3 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts the date of registration itself as the first of the fifteen days. The period runs from and excluding the trigger date.

questions.stem: On the security, the licence and the transporter's ₹14,00,000 claim, the correct position after conversion is:

options.text: The subsisting charge bars the conversion, so none of the other questions arises
options.explanation: The 'no security interest' condition belongs to the Third and Fourth Schedules and applies to a converting COMPANY. A firm converting under the Second Schedule is not caught by it.

options.text: The charge is no bar to a firm converting; the lease and the pending suit pass to the LLP by operation of s. 58(3)(b) and s. 58(4); the excise licence transfers only subject to the provisions of the excise statute under s. 58(5); and the four former partners remain personally liable for the pre-conversion claim
options.explanation: Correct. Each limb comes from a different sub-section, and the last is the point students miss: conversion gives prospective protection only, and the Second Schedule preserves the partners' liability for obligations incurred before conversion.

options.text: Every asset and every licence vests in the LLP automatically and without any further step under any law
options.explanation: Section 58(5) makes the transfer of an approval, permit or licence subject to the provisions of the Act under which it was issued, so a sectoral formality may still be required.

options.text: The 2024 suit abates, because the firm is deemed dissolved under s. 58(3)(c)
options.explanation: Section 58(4) expressly allows pending proceedings to be continued, completed and enforced by or against the LLP.

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 3, 4, 26, 28 · LLP and a partnership firm
questions.stem: Distinguish between a limited liability partnership and a partnership firm constituted under the Indian Partnership Act 1932. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: LLP compared with a partnership firm →

skeleton.point: Governing law and legal status: a firm is governed by the Indian Partnership Act 1932 and has no separate legal existence from its partners; an LLP is governed by the LLP Act 2008, is a body corporate and a legal entity separate from its partners, and the 1932 Act does not apply to it

Creation and perpetual succession: a firm arises from agreement and registration is optional, while an LLP comes into existence only on registration; a firm has no perpetual succession, whereas a change in the partners of an LLP does not affect its existence, rights or liabilities

Liability and agency: every partner of a firm is liable jointly and severally, personally and without limit, because he is the agent of the firm AND of the other partners; a partner of an LLP is the agent of the LLP but NOT of the other partners, an obligation of the LLP is solely its own, and a partner is not personally liable merely by being a partner

Number and eligibility of partners: a firm is capped at 50 persons and a minor may be admitted to the benefits of partnership, whereas an LLP has a minimum of two partners and no maximum, may have a body corporate as a partner, and has no provision for a minor

Compliance and publicity: a firm files no accounts and needs no audit under the 1932 Act, while an LLP must file a Statement of Account and Solvency and an annual return, must have its accounts audited above the prescribed thresholds, and its filings are open to public inspection

questions.stem: State the salient features of a limited liability partnership under the LLP Act 2008. (5 marks)

readLink.label: Read: What an LLP is →

skeleton.point: Body corporate and separate legal entity, formed and incorporated under the Act, with perpetual succession, and a change in partners does not affect its existence, rights or liabilities
The Indian Partnership Act 1932 does not apply to an LLP, and the LLP comes into existence only on registration, the certificate of incorporation being conclusive evidence of it

Minimum of two partners with no maximum; at least two designated partners who are individuals, of whom at least one must be resident in India; a body corporate may be a partner but not a designated partner

Every partner is the agent of the LLP but not of the other partners; an obligation of the LLP is solely the obligation of the LLP, met out of its property, and a partner is not personally liable for it solely by reason of being a partner
Mutual rights and duties are governed by the LLP agreement, with the First Schedule supplying the default on any matter the agreement does not deal with

It may sue and be sued, own property and have a common seal if it decides to have one; contribution may be in cash or kind including services; and it must file a Statement of Account and Solvency and an annual return each year

questions.stem: Explain the procedure for the incorporation of a limited liability partnership under sections 11 and 12 of the LLP Act 2008, and state the effect of registration. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Incorporation →

skeleton.point: Two or more persons associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit subscribe their names to an incorporation document
The incorporation document is filed with the Registrar of the State in which the registered office is to be situated, in the prescribed manner and with the prescribed fee

A statement that all the requirements of the Act and the rules have been complied with is filed along with it, made by an advocate, Company Secretary, Chartered Accountant or Cost Accountant engaged in the formation of the LLP AND by a subscriber to the incorporation document

Contents of the incorporation document: the prescribed form, the name, the proposed business, the address of the registered office, the names and addresses of the persons who are to be partners and of those who are to be designated partners, and such other prescribed information

The Registrar registers the document and issues a certificate of incorporation within fourteen days; he may accept the s. 11(1)(c) statement as sufficient evidence of compliance; the certificate is signed and sealed by him and is CONCLUSIVE EVIDENCE that the LLP is incorporated by the name specified in it

Effect of registration: the LLP by its name may sue and be sued, acquire, own, hold, develop and dispose of movable and immovable, tangible and intangible property, have a common seal if it decides to have one, and do and suffer such other acts as bodies corporate may lawfully do and suffer

questions.topic: Ch 5 · s. 23, First Schedule · Default provisions
questions.stem: In the absence of any provision in the LLP agreement, how are the mutual rights and duties of the partners of an LLP determined? State any six of the default provisions that then apply. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: The LLP agreement and the First Schedule →

skeleton.point: Section 23(1) makes the LLP agreement the governing instrument, and section 23(4) provides that in the absence of agreement as to any matter the mutual rights and duties are determined by the provisions relating to that matter set out in the First Schedule — so the Schedule operates matter by matter, not all or nothing
All the partners are entitled to share EQUALLY in the capital, profits and losses of the LLP, whatever each has contributed

The LLP indemnifies each partner for payments made and personal liabilities incurred in the ordinary and proper conduct of the business or in anything necessarily done to preserve the business or property; and every partner indemnifies the LLP for loss caused by his fraud
Every partner may take part in the management of the LLP, and no partner is entitled to remuneration for acting in the business or management of the LLP
No person may be introduced as a partner without the consent of all the existing partners

Ordinary matters are decided by a resolution passed by a majority in NUMBER of the partners, each partner having one vote, but no change may be made in the nature of the business without the consent of all partners; decisions are minuted within thirty days and kept at the registered office

A partner must render true accounts and full information, must account for the profits of a competing business carried on without consent and for any benefit derived without consent from the LLP's transactions, property, name or business connection

No partner may be expelled by a majority unless an express power of expulsion has been conferred by agreement, and unresolved disputes between partners go to arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996

questions.topic: Ch 5 · ss. 26 to 30 · Extent of liability
questions.stem: Explain the extent of the liability of a limited liability partnership and of its partners under sections 26 to 30 of the LLP Act 2008, and state the circumstances in which a partner may nevertheless be made personally liable. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Extent of liability of the LLP and of a partner →
