skeleton.point: Section 26: every partner is, for the purpose of the business of the LLP, the agent of the LLP but NOT of the other partners — the structural difference from s. 18 of the Partnership Act 1932 from which limited liability follows

Section 27(1): the LLP is not bound by what a partner does only where the partner in fact had no authority AND the person dealing with him knew that, or did not know or believe him to be a partner — both limbs are required

Section 27(2) to (4): the LLP is liable where a partner is liable to any person for a wrongful act or omission in the course of its business or with its authority; an obligation of the LLP, whether in contract or otherwise, is SOLELY the obligation of the LLP, met out of the property of the LLP

Section 28: a partner is not personally liable for such an obligation solely by reason of being a partner, but he remains personally liable for his OWN wrongful act or omission and is never personally liable for the wrongful act or omission of another partner

Section 29 (holding out): a person who represents himself, or knowingly permits himself to be represented, as a partner is liable to anyone who gave credit to the LLP on the faith of it, whether or not he knew the representation had reached that person; the LLP is liable in addition to the extent of the credit received or benefit derived; and the estate of a deceased partner is not liable merely because the LLP name continues

Section 30 (fraud): where an act is done by the LLP or a partner with intent to defraud creditors or for a fraudulent purpose, the liability of the LLP and of the partners who so acted is UNLIMITED, the LLP escaping only if it establishes that the act was without its knowledge or authority; with imprisonment up to five years and fine of ₹50,000 to ₹5,00,000 for a person knowingly a party, and compensation under s. 30(3)
Other routes to personal liability: the knowing sole partner after six months under s. 6(2), and a designated partner's liability for penalties imposed on the LLP under s. 8(b)

questions.stem: Who is a designated partner? State the requirements as to their appointment, the identification number they must obtain, their liabilities, and what happens when a vacancy arises. (5 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Designated partners and the DPIN →

skeleton.point: Meaning: a designated partner is a partner designated as such pursuant to section 7; the status is a compliance burden, not a superior class of ownership

Every LLP must have at least two designated partners who are INDIVIDUALS, at least one of whom is resident in India, meaning a person who has stayed in India for not less than 120 days during the financial year; where all or some of the partners are bodies corporate, at least two individuals who are partners or nominees of those bodies corporate act as designated partners

Appointment may be by the incorporation document naming them, or by the incorporation document providing that every partner from time to time is a designated partner, or by a partner becoming one in accordance with the LLP agreement; prior consent in the prescribed form is required, and the LLP files the particulars of every consenting individual within thirty days of his appointment
Every designated partner must obtain a Designated Partner Identification Number from the Central Government, sections 153 to 159 of the Companies Act 2013 applying mutatis mutandis

Liabilities: a designated partner is responsible for the doing of all acts required to be done by the LLP to comply with the Act, including the filing of documents, returns, statements and reports and as specified in the LLP agreement, and is liable to ALL penalties imposed on the LLP for contravening those provisions

Vacancy: the LLP may appoint a designated partner within thirty days of a vacancy arising for any reason; if none is appointed, or if at any time there is only one designated partner, EVERY partner is deemed to be a designated partner; contravention of s. 7(1) attracts a penalty of ₹10,000 and of ss. 7(4), 7(5) or 9 a penalty of ₹5,000, with ₹100 for each further day and the prescribed maximums

questions.stem: A private company wishes to convert itself into a limited liability partnership. State the conditions it must satisfy and the effect of registration of the conversion. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Conversion into an LLP →

skeleton.point: Enabling provision: a private company may convert into an LLP in accordance with Chapter X and the Third Schedule; a firm converts under s. 55 and the Second Schedule and an unlisted public company under s. 57 and the Fourth Schedule, but a LISTED public company cannot convert at all

The two cumulative conditions in the Third Schedule: there must be no security interest in the assets of the company subsisting or in force at the time of the application, and the partners of the LLP must comprise all the shareholders of the company and no one else
On being satisfied of compliance, the Registrar registers the documents and issues a certificate of registration stating that the LLP is registered under the Act on and from the date specified in it
The LLP must inform the concerned Registrar of Companies of the conversion and of its particulars within fifteen days of the date of registration

Effect: on and from that date there is an LLP by the name specified; all tangible and intangible property, assets, interests, rights, privileges, liabilities and obligations and the whole undertaking of the company are transferred to and vest in the LLP WITHOUT FURTHER ASSURANCE, ACT OR DEED; and the company is deemed to be dissolved and removed from the records of the Registrar of Companies

Continuity and limits: pending proceedings may be continued, completed and enforced by or against the LLP, contracts of employment continue, and existing agreements, deeds and instruments remain in force as if the LLP were a party; approvals, permits and licences transfer only SUBJECT TO the provisions of the Act under which they were issued; and the LLP must carry a statement of the conversion on its official correspondence for twelve months, beginning not later than fourteen days after registration
